extracted.intended_audience: Authors of research software papers, potential JOSS reviewers, and editors (research software developers seeking to publish in JOSS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for preparing, submitting, and reviewing research-software papers for the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS), including scope, review expectations, ethics, and policies (e.g., AI use, licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of research software (in-scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS publishes articles about research software. This definition includes software that: solves complex modeling problems in a scientific context (physics, mathematics, biology, medicine, social science, neuroscience, engineering); supports the functioning of research instruments or the execution of research experiments; extracts knowledge from large data sets; offers a mathematical library, or similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While useful for many areas of research, pre-trained machine learning models and notebooks are not in-scope for JOSS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and significance (scholarly contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software should demonstrate clear research impact or credible scholarly significance and represent a meaningful contribution to the research community rather than being a one-off tool for a single analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS evaluates submissions based on evidence of research impact, intellectual contribution, and good open-source practices; software must be more than a minor utility and should be likely to be cited by other researchers in the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of research impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should provide evidence of research impact such as publications or analyses using the software, external adopters or integrations, or credible near-term significance demonstrated through benchmarks and reproducible materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and editors consider concrete evidence (citations, integrations, benchmarks, reproducible examples) when assessing impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design thinking and architectural decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Software should show meaningful architectural decisions, trade-offs considered, and conceptual frameworks that capture domain expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS values work that builds upon existing software ecosystems rather than reinventing solutions; describe design decisions and why they were made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open development practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should demonstrate open development: sustained development over time with evidence of collaborative effort, public development history, comprehensive testing, clear documentation, and pathways for community contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence can include public commits, tests, continuous integration, documentation, issue/PR activity, contributor diversity; lack of these is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness and likelihood of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should be sufficiently useful that it is likely to be cited by other researchers in the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider whether the software addresses real needs in the field and whether others will realistically reuse or cite it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-complete and designed for maintainable extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must be feature-complete (i.e., no half-baked solutions) and designed for maintainable extension (not one-off modifications of existing tools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor 'utility' packages, including 'thin' API clients, and single-function packages are not acceptable; authors should avoid submitting underdeveloped or narrowly bespoke code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public development history requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects developed privately are not eligible until there is a public record of open development: at least six months of public history prior to submission, with evidence of releases, public issues/pull requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A history of contributions and engagement from individuals beyond the original team is especially welcome, though not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source licensing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS submissions must be open source (i.e., have an OSI-approved license).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the repository has an explicit OSI-approved license before submission; otherwise the submission is out-of-scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web-based software: core library or high rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Many web-based research tools are out of scope unless they meet one or both criteria: 1) they are built around and expose a 'core library' through a web-based experience (e.g., R/Shiny applications), or 2) the web application demonstrates a high-level of rigor with respect to domain modeling and testing (e.g., adopts and implements a design pattern such as MVC using a framework such as Django).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of web-based tools should emphasize modularity, testability, and an exposed library/API to make the project suitable for JOSS.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage policy — author disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of generative AI is permitted for most aspects of a JOSS submission, but all such use must be disclosed in an 'AI usage disclosure' statement which includes: tools/models used (and versions) and where they were used (code, paper text, docs); the nature and scope of assistance (e.g., code generation, refactoring, test scaffolding, copy-editing, drafting); and confirmation that human authors reviewed, edited, validated all AI-assisted outputs and made the core design decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI is not allowed for conversational interactions between authors and editors or reviewers unless used for translation. Authors remain fully responsible for accuracy, originality, licensing, and ethical/legal compliance. Failure to disclose can lead to desk rejection, mandatory revisions, or post-publication correction/withdrawal and could trigger institutional notification in cases of intentional misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage policy — reviewer use and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may use generative AI tools to assist with non-substantive tasks (e.g., grammar checks of their review text, contextualizing public materials and code snippets) and must disclose this briefly at the end of their review. The reviewer — not the AI — owns the evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All judgements, recommendations, and technical claims must be the reviewer's and verified by them. Human reviewers must make all evaluative decisions (scoring, accept/reject recommendations, assessments of originality, novelty, correctness, significance, and policy/ethics compliance). AI may assist analysis but must not render or determine verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review scope and process (what reviewers assess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the paper and the software are reviewed: reviewers evaluate the quality, documentation, and design of the software as well as the accuracy and completeness of the paper itself. Reviews take place openly via public GitHub issues in the JOSS reviews repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full review record (reviewer comments, author responses, editorial decisions) is permanently and publicly accessible. See JOSS reviewer guidelines and review criteria for full details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conduct: objectivity, conflicts, and citation suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments should be objective. JOSS reviewers should ideally have no conflict of interest. If a reviewer has a conflict of interest, it must be declared and recorded; editors may waive it in some cases. Reviewers should point out relevant published work which is not yet cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews are public and non-anonymous while in progress and post-review; transparency is an expected norm. Examples of misconduct include suggesting non-real reviewers or undisclosed conflicts; such things must be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: plagiarism, self-plagiarism, authorship, and review integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism (including copyright violation) for both software and papers is not allowed. Self-plagiarism (repeated publication of the same work) is not allowed. Author lists must be correct and complete; all listed authors must have made a contribution and significant contributors should be included. Reviews should be accurate and non-fraudulent. Reviewers and editors must disclose conflicts. Bribes are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of misconduct are handled by the Open Journals ethics team and may lead to corrections, retractions, and notifying institutions or funders. Authors are obliged to provide retractions or corrections of mistakes they become aware of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author responsibilities and submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are obliged to participate in peer review, ensure all authors have significantly contributed, and the submitting author must be a major contributor to the software. JOSS papers are required to have a list of references and financial support statements. It is forbidden to publish the same research in more than one journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review process includes a check that 'the full list of paper authors seems appropriate and complete.' Authors must correct the record if mistakes are found post-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and retractions process
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor fixes are processed by the Editors-in-Chief and handled publicly based on requests from the original authors (managed in the GitHub review linked from the paper). Major corrections will be reviewed by the EiC and ethics team and, if accepted, the paper will be re-published with an editorial note on the GitHub review. Retractions are considered by the EiC team and the ethics team; if warranted, a retraction notice will be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the editorial workflow and transparency for post-publication changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content licensing specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS is diamond/platinum open access. Copyright of JOSS papers is retained by submitting authors and accepted papers are subject to a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). Any code snippets included in JOSS papers are subject to the MIT license regardless of the license of the submitted software package under review. Any use of the JOSS logo is licensed CC BY 4.0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be aware of these licensing decisions when preparing papers and including code snippets or logos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archiving and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS articles, metadata, and reviews are archived with Portico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures long-term preservation of published content; authors and editors should be aware of the archiving policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of operations and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS publishes full submission and publication analytics and a detailed breakdown of running costs; it automates routine editorial work so editors can focus on review quality and keeps operations transparent and low-cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal operates with volunteers and under NumFOCUS fiscal sponsorship. This is procedural guidance explaining sustainability practices rather than acceptance criteria, but it underpins expectations about the journal's openness and transparency.
